care: Tacitus writes about cruel emperors, treason trials, murders at court, wars and a civil war. He describes some of this vividly. The lesson names these events without detail. Young readers can start with the shape of the story and with the question Tacitus raises: how do you write history fairly?

young.html: Tacitus was a Roman senator who wrote the history of the first emperors after Augustus. He lived through hard times himself: under one emperor, senators were afraid to speak their minds. When better times came, he wrote down what had happened, so that people would remember.

Tacitus promised to write about the past “without anger and without partiality”, which means without letting his own feelings, or his friends and enemies, bend the truth. That is a hard promise to keep, and readers still argue about whether he kept it.

Two sides of one story. Think of a small argument that happened in your family or class, such as who got the last cookie. Write what happened in two short versions: one by someone who was upset, one by someone calm and fair. Underline the words in each version that show feelings (“grabbed,” “selfish,” “just took one”). Which version would a good historian trust more, and why?

young.cap: The emperors Tacitus wrote about. Tap a bar to learn about each one. Some parts of his books are lost.

full.html: Cornelius Tacitus (c. AD 56–c. 120) came from a family outside Rome, probably in Gaul or northern Italy, and rose through the offices of state to become consul in AD 97 and later governor of the province of Asia. He married the daughter of Agricola, the general who governed Britain. He served under the emperor Domitian (AD 81–96), whose last years were a time of fear for the senate, and began writing when Nerva and Trajan came to power.

He wrote two great histories. The Histories (written around AD 100–110) told the story from the civil war of AD 69 to Domitian’s death in 96. The Annals, written later, went back to AD 14 and covered the emperors Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero. Neither survives complete: we have about a third of the Histories and a little over half of the Annals.

full.name: gb-emperors
full.cap: The emperors from AD 14 to 96, and how much of Tacitus survives for each. Tap a bar.

full.html: The Annals open with a short sketch of Rome from the kings to Augustus, then Tacitus explains why a new history is needed.

full.text: The histories of Tiberius, Caius, Claudius, and Nero, while they were in power, were falsified through terror, and after their death were written under the irritation of a recent hatred. Hence my purpose is to relate a few facts about Augustus—more particularly his last acts, then the reign of Tiberius, and all which follows, without either bitterness or partiality, from any motives to which I am far removed.
full.author: Tacitus
full.tr: Alfred John Church and William Jackson Brodribb

full.html: In Latin the promise is four words: sine ira et studio, “without anger and without partiality” (or zeal). Tacitus names the two ways history goes wrong: flattery while a ruler lives, and hatred after he dies.
The Histories begin the same way, then warn the reader what is coming.

full.text:
Those who profess inviolable truthfulness must speak of all without partiality and without hatred. …

I am entering on the history of a period rich in disasters, frightful in its wars, torn by civil strife, and even in peace full of horrors. Four emperors perished by the sword.
full.author: Tacitus
full.tr: Alfred John Church and William Jackson Brodribb
full.note: Church and Brodribb’s History was first published in 1864.

full.text: What the Annals and Histories tell

items: Tiberius (AD 14–37): Germanicus, the popular general, dies in the East; the ambitious minister Sejanus rises and falls; treason trials make the senate afraid. Tacitus shows an able ruler growing more suspicious and remote.
Claudius (41–54): the surviving books show a court run by his wives and freed slaves, and the conquest of Britain.

Nero (54–68): good early years under the advice of Seneca; then crimes within his own family, the great fire of Rome in AD 64 and a failed plot against him. Tacitus records that Nero blamed the fire on the Christians, one of the earliest mentions of Christ by a writer who was not a Christian.
The year of the four emperors (AD 69): Galba, Otho and Vitellius each seize power and fall within months, until Vespasian ends the civil war.
Rome’s frontiers: the revolt of the British queen Boudica (AD 60–61), wars in Germany and Armenia, and a revolt on the Rhine.

full.html: Tacitus is famous for short, sharp sentences that pack a judgment into a few words. Of Galba he wrote that everyone would have thought him fit to rule, had he never ruled. In the Annals he remarks that the more corrupt the state, the more numerous its laws (corruptissima re publica plurimae leges). He often reports what people suspected or rumored, which lets him hint at a judgment without stating it.

Taking every judgment in Tacitus as plain fact. He was a senator writing about emperors, and his sympathies lie with the senate. He sometimes reports a rumor and then lets it color the reader’s view. Historians compare him with other sources, such as the biographer Suetonius, inscriptions and coins. Most still regard him as the greatest Roman historian, and also as one who must be read carefully.

items: History writing: “without anger and without partiality” became a motto for historians, even those who think no one fully achieves it.
Freedom: readers in later centuries, living under kings, found in Tacitus a study of how power works, and how flattery and fear destroy free speech.
Survival: Books 1–6 of the Annals survive in a single medieval manuscript, and Books 11–16 with the Histories in another. Without them we would know far less about the first century AD.

deep.text: Context: writing after a time of fear

deep.html: In his short Agricola (AD 98), Tacitus says that under Domitian Romans lost the very memory of free speech, and that they would have lost memory itself if forgetting were as easy as keeping silent. His histories are, in part, an effort to remember. In the same book he gives a British chief a famous line about Roman conquest: “they make a desert and call it peace” (solitudinem faciunt, pacem appellant). Ancient historians often wrote such speeches themselves, and Tacitus’s willingness to voice Rome’s enemies is part of what makes him interesting.

items: Can anyone write about people they lived through, or suffered under, without anger or partiality?
Is it fair for a historian to report rumors? When is a rumor itself an important fact?
Why might people under a powerful ruler stop telling the truth, even when no one forces them to lie?
Tacitus served Domitian and did well under him, and later wrote against him. What should a good person do under a bad government?

deep.html: Gibbon’s Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, later on this ladder, admired Tacitus and took up the story where the great Roman historians left off. Montesquieu drew on him for his studies of Roman greatness and of liberty. Readers have long disagreed over whether Tacitus teaches how to resist tyranny or how to survive it.

questions: What does it mean to write “without anger and without partiality”? Is it possible?
Why might history written while a ruler is alive be different from history written after he dies?
When you hear two versions of the same story, how do you decide which to trust?
Tacitus says fear made people stop speaking freely. Have you ever kept quiet because you were afraid of what others would think? What happened?
Much of Tacitus is lost. What would you most want to be remembered from our own time, and how could we make sure it survives?
